article.headline: dmux Frees AI Coding Agents From the Terminal Window
article.lede: Every developer who has left a long job in a terminal knows the dread of an accidental window close. dmux, announced by @jpschroeder, addresses this directly for AI coding agents — the autonomous programs that now handle multi-hour programming tasks on a developer's behalf. The tool does not reinvent anything; it packages an old Unix capability into a workflow built for a new kind of workload.
article.body:
The foundation is **tmux**, a *terminal multiplexer* that has been part of the Unix toolkit for well over a decade. tmux runs as a server process that communicates with terminal windows — its clients — through a socket, typically in /tmp on Linux systems. When a terminal window closes, only the client connection drops; the server and everything running inside it continues uninterrupted. Sessions can be detached deliberately or survive accidental disconnection, and reattaching restores the state exactly as it was left.

dmux wraps this behavior into a single command aimed at a specific audience. Closing the terminal no longer signals doom for whatever the agent was doing mid-task. The tweet's numbered list — tmux runs as a background server, terminal closing doesn't kill tmux, type `dmux` to return — is essentially a consumer-friendly restatement of how tmux has always worked, packaged for developers who may not have grown up with it.

The screenshot attached to the post makes the use case concrete. A dmux session shows a coding agent in the middle of substantial autonomous work: running Playwright browser tests, benchmarking JavaScript frameworks (Arrow against Vue), updating package sandboxes, managing multiple git worktrees, and verifying type-checking passes — all without human supervision across what appears to be an extended session. The session label "agentbuilder-coordinator" suggests dmux is organizing multiple concurrent agent workstreams, not just a single terminal.

The appeal is not technical novelty — tmux's persistence model is well-understood and unchanged — but *ergonomics*. AI coding agents increasingly run tasks that take minutes to hours: cloning repositories, iterating on benchmarks, running full test suites. Tying those processes to a fragile terminal window creates unnecessary risk. dmux reframes tmux's existing capability as a feature explicitly designed for this new class of long-running, autonomous workload.

concepts.definition: A program that lets one terminal window host multiple independent shell sessions simultaneously. tmux is the dominant example: it runs as a background server so sessions outlive the terminal window that created them, and any number of clients can attach to or detach from the same session.

tmux separates the server (which manages sessions and processes) from the client (the terminal window the user sees). They communicate via a Unix socket, usually in /tmp. Closing the client severs the display connection but leaves the server — and everything running on it — completely intact.

An autonomous program, typically backed by a large language model, that can plan and execute multi-step software tasks — running tests, editing files, reading documentation — with minimal human intervention. Because these tasks can run for many minutes, they are especially vulnerable to losing state when a terminal closes.

A software construct that emulates a hardware terminal, allowing programs to read from and write to what looks like a serial line. tmux manages sessions through ptys, which is why processes inside tmux behave exactly as if they were attached to a real terminal — even when no terminal window is open.
